extracted.intended_audience: aspiring TV writers and comedy writers (people trying to break into writers' rooms)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical advice and norms for getting a job and functioning effectively in a TV writers' room, with an emphasis on comedy-room behavior, pitching, networking, and script preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writers are the be-all and end-all
rubrics_metrics.description: "In TV, the writers are the be-all and end-all. They decide what happens in every episode of every season, and they are even the final word on a set. A scene isn’t done shooting until the writer tells the director they are clear to move on. Unlike feature films, where the director takes over as soon as the studio buys the writer’s script, in TV the director is a hired gun." (5)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes that writers hold ultimate creative authority in TV; implies writers must own decisions, be present/available for production, and understand their continuing role beyond script delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: A great script needs the right reader
rubrics_metrics.description: "A great script isn’t anything if the right person isn’t reading it." (12)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights the importance of targeting and getting your script into the hands of decision-makers; networking and timing are evaluative factors as important as script quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be quick with great jokes in a comedy room
rubrics_metrics.description: "In a comedy room, a successful staff writer is often one who is quick with a great joke that keeps the room from getting stuck. A good story pitch gets tossed and turned around in the room, and it’s hard for the showrunner to decipher who it came from or where it started. But a good joke gets credit immediately. And when you’re in this position, credit is important." (38)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance in the room (speed and punchiness of jokes) is a measurable criterion for success in comedy rooms; getting credit for jokes matters for career advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match pitching frequency to the next level up
rubrics_metrics.description: "When entering a new room, it’s best to gauge the next level writer up from you, see how much they’re pitching, and mimic their frequency. They can’t fault you if you’re a staff writer and you’re speaking as much as the story editor. But if you’re talking as much as a co-executive producer or the show runner, you should probably chill out for a few weeks until you get a feel for the room." (66)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioral norm: calibrate participation to hierarchy; avoid over-talking relative to senior writers until you understand room dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit persistent pitching to two extra tries
rubrics_metrics.description: "If you don’t feel that strongly about the pitch, let it go. But if you do feel that this is important for the show, here’s how to approach it. The general rule is that you get two more cracks at it. The second time, you can reiterate your point, present it in a slightly different way, and explain why this is important. If it gets shot down again, then you’re playing with fire. But if it’s important to you and you really need to get your point across, you can give an 'I’m sorry, I’m going to pitch this one more time and then I’ll drop it, but it’s really important to me that..' This shows that you’re aware that you’re harping on the same point, and you feel it’s important enough to pitch again." (66)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a concrete pitching etiquette rule: two reiterations allowed, third try needs explicit framing and acknowledgement; otherwise stop to avoid damaging relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer non-pitch 'general area' ideas only at impasse
rubrics_metrics.description: "There may be a time in a writers’ room when a particular plot point is giving everyone trouble. And maybe a fresh framework could shake things up. In that case, it’s perfectly okay to say 'Is it all right if I pitch a general area?' or something to that effect. That way, the room is aware that you know you’re not providing a pitch, just an interesting idea that may help the room break through whatever’s holding them back.' However, that should only a be employed when it’s clear that the room is at an impasse." (67)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use broad, exploratory contributions sparingly and only when the room is stuck; label them as such so you don't overstep expectations about delivering polished pitches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the flow of the room
rubrics_metrics.description: "More than anything, it’s important to follow the flow of the room." (67)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority guideline: adapt to the room’s momentum and direction; avoid derailing productive sessions by rehashing settled ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t derail rooms that are 'in the zone'
rubrics_metrics.description: "When a room is really moving, dialogue, story ideas, and character moves flow easily. A good showrunner will follow the direction a story is going and will dictate where to go next. That’s why it’s so important to follow the showrunner’s lead and not go backwards. Rooms that are in the zone can be turned upside-down by somebody saying 'Can we go back for a second?'" (67)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect momentum: avoid backtracking when the room has strong forward motion; follow showrunner leadership to preserve productive energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute and protect colleagues' ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: "When you know you’re using a piece of someone else’s idea for your pitch, use a 'bouncing off of what [writer who was being ignored] was saying' to frame your pitch. This keeps that person in the game. Also, if you hear an idea being taken and repurposed as their own, feel free to call it out. It doesn’t have to be offensive. It can be as simple as 'Right, that was a great pitch by (ignored writer].'" (68)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice generous attribution to preserve collegiality and fairness; courteously reclaim or credit ideas when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain and add to your network
rubrics_metrics.description: "Your goal should always be to maintain and add to your network." (89)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Networking is an ongoing evaluative and practical activity; relationships are part of career success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask for what you want and follow up
rubrics_metrics.description: "The only people who get what they want are the people who ask for what they want. So, keep following up with people and keep them aware of what you’re looking for." (89)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactive self-advocacy and persistent follow-up are recommended behaviors to secure opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script draft color order
rubrics_metrics.description: "With each new revision, a new color is given to the pages of the script, and those colors are nearly identical across all TV shows. In draft order, it goes like this: White (this is the first draft of any script) Blue Pink Yellow Green Goldenrod Buff Salmon Cherry Double White Double Blue (and on and on)" (115)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical production convention: know and follow the page-coloring system for drafts to align with industry expectations and logistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence: keep writing rather than expecting success
rubrics_metrics.description: "At the end of the day, you can’t expect success. You have to go in with the mentality of 'How do I just keep writing?'" (140)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes sustained output and resilience as primary career strategy rather than reliance on luck.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make dedicated, regular writing time
rubrics_metrics.description: "I took freelance jobs in advertising, and I made time to write six nights a week—usually from 11:30 p.m. to 1:30 a.m., at a minimum. Every single night after my wife went to bed, I was writing." -Howard Jordan Jr. (149)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete habit: set regular blocks of late-night (or otherwise consistent) time to write; treat writing as scheduled work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply targeted notes: push stories up; differentiate voices; keep specs focused
rubrics_metrics.description: "she gave me three sentences of notes: push all your stories up, your characters all sound the same (they speak in the same rhythmic pattern), and if you’re gonna do a spec, then don’t get so creative that the supporting characters are the stars of the show." -Howard Jordan Jr. (149)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial criteria: increase story momentum ('push up'), ensure distinct character voices, and in specs keep focus on protagonists rather than side characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write a story only you can write
rubrics_metrics.description: "What I say so often now is, write a story that only you can write in a way that only you can write it. I noticed that people had mastered that presentation of self. I’ve always sold brands; l’ve never had to sell me." -Howard Jordan Jr. (150)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality and authentic voice are key differentiators; develop a unique personal angle in your stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volunteer to write on the board
rubrics_metrics.description: "volunteer to write on the board (because it might be the only time you get to speak)." -Howard Jordan Jr. (151)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactical advice: take visible, concrete actions (recording ideas on the board) to ensure participation and presence in the room.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation and room image matter
rubrics_metrics.description: "presentation matters, your room image matters." -Howard Jordan Jr. (151)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of writers include how they present themselves and how they are perceived in the room; polish and professionalism affect opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only ~20% of the job is writing
rubrics_metrics.description: "realize and accept that only 20 percent of the job is writing-if that." -Howard Jordan Jr. (151)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Career reality: many non-writing responsibilities (networking, meetings, pitching, production) factor into success; evaluate time allocation accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have conviction when pursuing creative opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: "I knew coming in that if there’s a one-in-a-million chance that this can be done, I’m that one. That’s the conviction you have to have when you pursue these creative endeavors, because creativity by nature is subjective." -Howard Jordan Jr. (152)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attitude criterion: confidence and persistence are necessary because subjective gatekeeping can obscure merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep improving; don’t rely on gatekeepers' imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: "Some of the arbiters of whether your great idea succeeds or not have no imagination. That doesn’t make you a bad writer. But it does mean you’re not getting hired. So, you have to figure out your way. You have to work so that you’re always getting better. Don’t keep writing the same version of the same script. Always work smarter." -Howard Jordan Jr. (152)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for career development: continuous improvement and strategic variation in your work to overcome conservative or unimaginative gatekeepers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be both a good writer and a good salesman
rubrics_metrics.description: "It’s not enough to just be a good writer. And it’s not enough to just be a good salesman. You have to have both, and you have to keep getting better at both." (152)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dual-skill requirement: craft and self-promotion/salesmanship are jointly necessary and are evaluative axes for hiring and advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showrunners want scripts that grab and start fast
rubrics_metrics.description: "WHAT SHOWRUNNERS LOOK FOR IN A WRITER The script has to grab me, and the story has to start real fast. If it doesn’t start by page four or five, I toss it and move on to the next one. Start fast. If it’s a comedy, you better hit me over the head with a big joke real fast, and those act break moments have to pop. I don’t even care if act three is no good. If acts one and two are good, we can fix act three." -Michael Jamin (173)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete evaluation standard from showrunners: fast opening (by p.4–5), strong early comedy beats and act breaks; early pages carry disproportionate weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Easier to break in now but harder to sustain a career
rubrics_metrics.description: "These days, I think it’s easier to break in, but harder to sustain a career." -Michael Jamin (176)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Market context: short-term entry opportunities may exist, but long-term career maintenance is challenging—implies evaluating long-term strategy and adaptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy careers have higher turnover and rely on room performance
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is much more turnover in comedy, and it is much harder to get your writing to stand out because so much is dictated by how you perform in the room." (188)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative axis: in comedy, interpersonal and in-room performance (not just script quality) is a major determinant of career stability and recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: TV hiring starts before public announcements
rubrics_metrics.description: "TV shows hire writers and form a writers’ room long before their announcement ever happens in Deadline. So, being in the know helps you get to the front of the line." (206)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry timing criterion: insider knowledge and early access to hiring information increase odds of getting hired; networking and information channels matter.
